Inventory notes:
- Demand is variable, typically 3–4 units/day, with spikes to 7–8; recent observations: 3, 7, 3, 4, 8, 0, 4, 4, 3.
- Stockouts are very expensive (about 3 per day plus lost sales), while holding cost is low (about 0.1 per unit) and each order costs 0.5. Favor maintaining safety stock rather than running near zero.
- Lead time appears to be up to 2 days. Include expected demand during the lead time and a buffer of roughly 3–5 units when deciding orders.
- Avoid delaying replenishment when on-hand inventory is below about 7–8 units, especially if arrivals are small or absent.
- Existing pipeline must be included: arrivals can prevent an order, but do not assume they fully cover demand plus safety stock.
- Ordering only 4 units at very low inventory led to stockouts during an 8-unit-demand day; later replenishment and larger orders reduced stockout risk.
- Counts have matched the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustment. Receiving temp staffing is a process-risk note, not proof of inventory error.
- Cycle-count scheduling has no immediate inventory implication.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is variable, usually 3–6 units/day, with spikes to 7–8; recent observations include 0 and several 5–6 days. Use roughly 4–5 units/day as baseline.
- Stockouts are very expensive (about 3–5+ per day plus lost sales); holding cost is low (~0.1/unit) and each order costs 0.5. Favor safety stock over lean inventory.
- Lead time appears to be up to 2 days. Cover expected demand during lead time plus roughly 3–5 units of safety stock.
- Evaluate total available inventory: on hand plus scheduled arrivals, but do not assume arrivals alone leave adequate safety stock. At low on-hand (especially below 7–8), replenish early.
- Recent stockouts occurred with on-hand 5 and no next-day arrival, and with zero on-hand despite orders that arrived later. A small order can be insufficient if the pipeline timing leaves a gap.
- Once arrivals were sufficient, orders of 4–6 units generally avoided stockouts, including several zero-on-hand cases. At zero on hand, order at least enough to cover the next demand window and restore buffer; do not delay merely because 4–6 units are already scheduled.
- Recent outcomes: orders of 4 with arrivals of 6/4 or 4/4 had no stockout; ordering 6 at on-hand 5 still incurred a stockout because near-term supply was absent. Timing matters more than order size alone.
- Counts have matched the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustment. Temporary receiving staff and racking changes are process-risk notes, not proof of inventory error.
- Carrier pickup timing and cycle-count scheduling have no demonstrated direct inventory effect, but monitor receiving execution when staffing or schedules change.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is variable, typically 3–6 units/day, with occasional 7–8; recent 14-day demand remains centered around 4–5/day.
- Stockouts are expensive (about 3–5+ per day plus lost sales), while holding cost is low (~0.1/unit) and each order costs 0.5. Favor safety stock over lean inventory.
- Lead time is up to 2 days. Target coverage of roughly 8–10 units (two days of demand plus 3–5 safety units), adjusted upward after recent stockouts.
- Evaluate on hand plus scheduled arrivals, but do not treat pipeline stock as immediately available. Same-day stockouts can occur even with 6–8 units arriving over the next two days.
- Repeated stockouts occurred at zero on hand on days 21–23 despite ordering 6, and again with on hand 2 plus arrivals of 4/5 on day 27. This confirms timing and near-term availability matter more than order size.
- When on hand is 0–3, order early and aggressively; do not delay because 4–6 units are already scheduled. Aim to restore at least a several-unit buffer after covering the next demand window. Orders of 6 prevented stockout on day 29 with zero on hand and arrivals of 8/6, but did not always do so under weaker timing.
- Recent no-stockout outcomes occurred with on hand 2–3 and arrivals totaling 10–12, and with zero on hand when near-term arrivals were stronger. Continue favoring orders around 4–8, increasing when pipeline timing is uncertain.
- Counts match the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustments. Temporary receiving staff, forklift certification, racking changes, carrier pickup timing, and cycle counts are process-risk notes only; monitor receiving execution but do not assume they affect inventory without evidence.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is usually 3–6/day, but recent spikes reached 10 and 14; plan for a normal rate around 5–6/day with spike protection.
- Stockouts are costly (~3–5+ per day plus lost sales), while holding cost is low (~0.1/unit) and each order costs 0.5. Favor safety stock over lean inventory.
- Lead time is up to 2 days. Pipeline inventory cannot be treated as immediately available; arrival timing matters more than total scheduled quantity.
- Recent stockouts occurred with zero on hand despite 6–10 units arriving over two days, and with 3 on hand plus 12 scheduled. Orders of 4–8 have not reliably prevented stockouts when the first arrival is delayed or demand spikes.
- When on hand is 0–3, order early and aggressively—generally 8 units or more when timing is uncertain or recent demand is elevated. Do not delay merely because 6–12 units are scheduled. Restore a several-unit immediately available buffer.
- A stronger position (zero on hand with 8+8 arriving, or 8 on hand with 8+8 arriving) avoided stockouts, but this is not guaranteed under high demand. Target roughly 10–14 units of effective coverage, adjusted upward after spikes or stockouts.
- Counts match the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustments. Racking changes, receiving staff, forklift certification, carrier pickup timing, and cycle counts are process-risk notes only. Monitor execution, but do not assume they alter inventory without evidence.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is typically 3–6/day, but spikes reached 10 and 14; recent demand remains elevated (roughly 5–8/day). Plan around 5–6/day with spike protection.
- Stockouts cost about 2+ per day plus lost sales, while holding cost is ~0.1/unit and each order costs 0.5. Favor adequate safety stock, but avoid unnecessary replenishment when coverage is strong.
- Lead time is up to 2 days. Pipeline inventory is not immediately available; arrival timing matters more than total scheduled quantity.
- Zero on hand with 6+8 or 8+10 arriving: ordering 10 maintained service through recent high demand. When on hand is 0–3, order early and generally 8–10+ if timing is uncertain or demand is elevated; do not wait merely because 6–12 units are scheduled.
- Recent runs show 14–19 on hand with arrivals and moderate demand can be allowed to deplete without ordering. On hand around 9–10 plus 8–10 arriving also avoided stockouts; ordering 0 at 9 with 8+8 pipeline was reasonable.
- Target roughly 10–14 units of effective near-term coverage, adjusted upward after spikes or stockouts. When on hand is 7–10 and arrivals total 16–18, an 8-unit order may be unnecessary unless demand accelerates or arrivals are unreliable. When on hand is ~18 with no pipeline, replenish about 8–10.
- Counts match the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustments. Racking changes, receiving staff, carrier pickup timing, forklift certification, and cycle counts remain process-risk notes only. Monitor execution, but do not assume they alter inventory without evidence.

Inventory notes:
- Demand has shifted higher: recent sales are commonly 8–12/day, with spikes to 11–12. Plan around 7–9/day rather than the older 5–6 baseline, with protection for 10–12.
- Stockouts remain costly (about 1–2+ per day plus lost sales), while ordering costs 0.5 and holding cost is relatively modest. Favor service protection when coverage is uncertain.
- Lead time is up to 2 days; pipeline inventory is not immediately usable, and arrival timing matters more than scheduled totals.
- When on hand is 0–3, order promptly—typically 8–10 or more—even with 18–20 units scheduled, especially after a sold-out day or during elevated demand. Recent zero-stock days with 8–10 arriving still required replenishment to avoid stockouts.
- When on hand is around 4–6 and demand is 8+, replenish if near-term arrivals may not cover consumption. Do not rely solely on one incoming shipment.
- When on hand is 9–10 with 16+ arriving, ordering 0 has avoided stockouts and is generally reasonable. Likewise, 13 on hand with 8 arriving did not require an order, though holding cost can be noticeable.
- Target roughly 10–14 units of effective near-term coverage; raise this toward 14–16 after consecutive high-demand or sold-out days. With around 18 on hand and no pipeline, replenish about 8–10.
- Recent counts matched the system; no evidence of shrinkage or adjustment. Receiving temps, racking changes, carrier timing, forklift certification, and cycle counts are process-risk notes only—monitor execution but do not assume they change inventory without evidence.

Inventory notes:
- Demand is elevated and volatile: typically 8–12/day, with recent spikes to 14. Plan around 8–10/day and protect for 12–14, especially after a high-demand or sold-out day.
- Stockouts are costly (about 1–2+ per day plus lost sales); ordering costs 0.5 and holding cost is modest. Favor service protection when coverage is uncertain.
- Lead time is up to 2 days. Pipeline inventory is not immediately usable; distinguish arrival day and do not rely on a single future shipment.
- With 0–3 on hand, order promptly—usually 10–12+—even with 18–22 scheduled. Recent 0-stock cases with 10–12 arriving still required replenishment.
- With 4–6 on hand, order roughly 8–12 when demand is elevated or the first arrival is not same-day. A 5-unit position with 9 arriving only on day 2 still suffered a stockout after 12 sales; a 4-unit position with 12 arriving day 2 also stocked out despite ordering 10.
- Orders of 8–10 were effective at 4 on hand with two 10-unit arrivals and at 2 on hand with 10 and 8 arriving. At 5 on hand with 9 and 10 arriving, ordering 0 worked, but this is not guaranteed under 12–14 demand.
- At 12 on hand with 8 arriving, ordering 0 was appropriate. Around 17 on hand with no pipeline, 0 may be sufficient; ordering 9 avoided stockout but incurred unnecessary ordering cost in that instance.
- Target about 10–14 units of effective near-term coverage; raise toward 14–16 after consecutive high-demand or sold-out days. With ~18 on hand and no pipeline, replenish about 8–10 if expected demand is high.
- Counts have matched the system. Operational notes (receiving temps, racking, carrier timing, certification, cycle counts) are process risks only; do not adjust inventory without evidence.
